title: If Your Spouse Dies, These 3 Things Happen to the Joint Account — Half of It Loses Cover

description:
Six months. That is how long the insurance on a joint bank account stays the way it was after one owner dies — and then it changes, without a letter, without a phone call, and without anybody at the bank being required to raise it.

A joint account is insured for $250,000 per owner. Two names, $500,000 protected. When one owner dies the FDIC keeps treating the account as though both were living, but only for six months. After that it becomes a single account with one limit. The FDIC's own example: a $500,000 joint account, one owner dies, nothing changed in six months — $250,000 uninsured.

Three things happen to a joint bank account when a husband or a wife dies:

1. The insurance holds for six months, then half of it is no longer covered
2. Closing the account is the common mistake — money is still arriving, bills are still leaving, and a closed account cannot be reopened
3. The protection that kept this money out of court came from the second name. With one name left, it is gone until a payable-on-death form puts it back

Everything here is the general federal rule on deposit insurance. Banks differ, states differ, and your own case is decided by the paperwork at your branch.
